text.hook:
Still writing mutex + condition_variable + counter for every handoff?

C++20 gave you latch, barrier, semaphore and jthread. The mental model, plus 6 myths. Save it. 📌
text.body:
Inside:
1. What state each primitive owns
2. Latch vs barrier in one slide
3. Semaphore vs mutex vs condition variable
4. The atomic::wait rules
5. What jthread really does at shutdown

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

first_comment: 🧠 Test yourself: can `latch.try_wait()` return false after the counter has already reached 0? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: Yes, with very low probability: the standard allows it. Fine in a `while (!l.try_wait())` loop, wrong as an "is it done?" check.

slides.lead: Primitives that carry their own state, and the myths that fail interviews.

slides.title: Each primitive owns its own state
slides.takeaway: All of them synchronize memory: writes before the signal are visible after the wait returns.

slides.title: One countdown vs repeated phases

cards.label: std::latch
cards.text: Any thread may `count_down()` or `wait()`. No reset: once at 0 it stays open forever.

cards.label: std::barrier
cards.text: The same N threads arrive every phase. A completion step runs once per phase, on one participant.

slides.takeaway: Workers' writes before `count_down()` are visible after `wait()`. No extra mutex to read results.

slides.title: Lock-step phases + completion
slides.takeaway: All arrivals happen before the completion step, so it can safely combine results.

slides.title: Permits with no owner

cards.label: vs mutex
cards.text: Any thread may `release()`. No `lock`/`unlock`, so `std::lock_guard` does not compile.

cards.label: vs condition variable
cards.text: The count remembers a release. Signal before anyone waits and it is not lost.

cards.label: Initial count
cards.text: `{0}` = signal not given yet. `{K}` = K permits free.

slides.takeaway: Semaphore for signalling and throttling. Mutex for exclusion.

slides.title: The four rules
items: It returns only after it sees a different value
Change the value first, then notify
A to B to A can be missed: use a generation counter
slides.takeaway: Lost-wakeup safe: the value check and going to sleep are atomic (futex semantics).

slides.title: RAII join + cooperative stop

cards.label: Cooperative
cards.text: Nothing is interrupted. The thread must poll its `stop_token` or wait in `condition_variable_any`.

slides.takeaway: As a class member, declare the `jthread` **last**: it starts last and is stopped and joined first.

items.myth: "A latch can be reset for the next round."
items.truth: It is one-shot. Use a new latch per round, or a `std::barrier`.

items.myth: "A latch only orders execution. I still need a mutex to read the results."
items.truth: Latch and barrier give happens-before for writes made before arriving.

items.myth: "A barrier's completion function runs on a separate thread."
items.truth: It runs on one of the participating threads, once per phase.
It has no owner. Use it for signalling, `std::mutex` for mutual exclusion.
It returns only after it sees a value different from `old`.
It sets a flag and runs callbacks. The thread must cooperate.

slides.hero:
Let the primitive
own the state.
Then you cannot
forget the predicate.
slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

text.hook:
Main waits for both workers in every round with a std::latch.
Round 1 prints the right answer. 🤔

What about rounds 2 and 3?
Comment your answer, then swipe ➜ to check it.
text.body: Find the bug before you swipe. It compiles cleanly with -Wall -Wextra.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: how do you make 4 worker threads start their work at the same instant with a std::latch? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: `std::latch start{1};` Each worker calls start.wait() first; main calls start.count_down() once, after creating all of them.

slides.title: 3 rounds, one latch. What happens?

bullets: After round 1 the counter is 0 and **stays** 0. There is no reset.
Round 2: if `wait()` runs first it returns at once, and main reads `results` while workers write: data race.
`count_down()` past 0 breaks its precondition: UB. libstdc++ drives the counter negative, so a later `wait()` can block forever.
Seen with GCC 11: usually a hang right after round 1, sometimes "round 2: 21" (stale) first.
slides.wrong: "A: the latch rearms after wait() returns"

slides.tip: Same threads, repeated phases? That is exactly what `std::barrier` is for.
slides.takeaway: Latches cannot be reset. Create one per round, or use a barrier.

text.hook:
A std::jthread goes out of scope while its worker is still looping.

What prints, and in what order? 🧵
Think it through, comment your answer, then swipe ➜
text.body: Slide 3 shows what changes if you swap jthread for std::thread.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: in which thread does a std::stop_callback run? And what if stop was already requested when you construct it? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: In the thread calling request_stop(), before that call returns. If stop was already requested, it runs immediately, inside the constructor.

slides.title: What prints, in what order?

slides.verdict: C. leaving scope, worker: stop seen, after scope
bullets: At the closing brace `~jthread` runs `request_stop()`, then `join()`.
The worker sees `stop_requested()` within about 1 ms, prints, returns.
Only then does `join()` return and main prints "after scope".
The token is passed automatically: the lambda's first parameter is a `std::stop_token`.
slides.wrong: "A: the loop never ends, so it hangs"

slides.title: Same scope, different thread type

columns.label: std::thread

slides.tip: A worker blocked in `std::condition_variable::wait` ignores `request_stop()`. Use `condition_variable_any` with the token.
slides.takeaway: jthread = request stop + join in the destructor. Cancellation is cooperative: the loop must check the token.

text.hook:
"binary_semaphore is just a lighter, faster mutex."
So someone swapped it in for std::mutex.

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: The difference is one word, and it decides which tool you reach for.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: two threads must print ping, pong, ping, pong... in strict alternation. How do you do it with semaphores only? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: Two binary_semaphores: ping_turn{1}, pong_turn{0}. Each thread acquires its own turn, prints, then releases the other's. The releaser is never the acquirer, which a mutex forbids.

slides.title:
A semaphore replaces the mutex.
What happens?

slides.verdict_sub: GCC: 'class std::counting_semaphore<1>' has no member named 'lock'
bullets: The deeper reason: a semaphore counts permits and has **no owner**.
A mutex has an owner that must unlock it.

slides.title: No owner: any thread may release
slides.tip: Great for signalling (start at `{0}`) and limiting concurrency to K. A stray `release()` silently "unlocks" it.
slides.takeaway: Semaphore = permits without ownership, for signalling. Mutex = ownership, for exclusion.
